payload.set_intro: A clinic phones a random sample of $5$ patients from a large list on which $30\%$ of the patients missed their last appointment. Let $X$ be the number of patients in the sample who missed an appointment. The probability distribution of $X$ is shown in the table.

stimulus.description: Probability distribution of X, the number of patients in the sample who missed an appointment

items.stem: What is the mean (expected value) of $X$? Round to two decimal places.

options.why: Reports the probability of one outcome instead of the mean of $X$.
The mean of a binomial random variable is $np = 5(0.3) = 1.5$; weighting each value of $X$ by its probability in the table gives the same value.
Uses $n(1-p)$, the expected number of patients who did not miss an appointment, instead of $np$.
Uses $n/2$, as if each outcome had probability $0.5$.

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is $1.50$. The mean of a binomial random variable is $np = 5(0.3) = 1.5$; weighting each value of $X$ by its probability in the table gives the same value.
$0.30$ is incorrect: Reports the probability of one outcome instead of the mean of $X$.
$3.50$ is incorrect: Uses $n(1-p)$, the expected number of patients who did not miss an appointment, instead of $np$.
$2.50$ is incorrect: Uses $n/2$, as if each outcome had probability $0.5$.

key_conditions.condition: the mean of a binomial random variable is n times p
key_conditions.evidence: the table gives the distribution and the stem gives n and the percent of the outcome of interest

misconceptions.description: reports p instead of the mean
reports n divided by two as the mean

verification.independent_path: the mean is recomputed as the sum of x times P(X = x) over the table and compared with n times p

items.stem: What is the probability that at least $2$ of the patients in the sample missed an appointment? Use the table and round to three decimal places.

options.why: Finds $P(X = 2)$ only, instead of the probability of $2$ or more.
Subtracts only $P(X=1)$ from $1$, forgetting to subtract $P(X=0)$ as well.
Finds $P(X > 2)$, leaving out the probability that $X = 2$.
$P(X \ge 2) = 1 - P(X=0) - P(X=1) = 1 - 0.1681 - 0.3601 \approx 0.472$, which equals the sum of the table probabilities from $x=2$ on.

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is $0.472$. $P(X \ge 2) = 1 - P(X=0) - P(X=1) = 1 - 0.1681 - 0.3601 \approx 0.472$, which equals the sum of the table probabilities from $x=2$ on.
$0.309$ is incorrect: Finds $P(X = 2)$ only, instead of the probability of $2$ or more.
$0.640$ is incorrect: Subtracts only $P(X=1)$ from $1$, forgetting to subtract $P(X=0)$ as well.
$0.163$ is incorrect: Finds $P(X > 2)$, leaving out the probability that $X = 2$.

uses exactly 2 instead of at least 2

items.stem: Which of the following is the correct interpretation of $P(X=0)$ in this context?

options.text: The chance that any one of the patients in a sample missed an appointment is $17\%$
options.why: Confuses $P(X=0)$ with the probability for one individual item; the probability for one patient is given in the scenario.

options.text: In about $17\%$ of all such random samples of $5$ patients, none of the patients would have missed an appointment
options.why: $P(X=0) \approx 0.1681$ is the long-run proportion of random samples of $5$ patients in which none of the patients missed an appointment.

options.text: In about $17\%$ of all such samples, all of the patients would have missed an appointment
options.why: Reverses the event: $X=0$ means none are of the stated kind, not all.

options.text: Exactly $17\%$ of the patients in every sample of $5$ missed an appointment
options.why: Reads a probability as a guaranteed percentage in every sample.

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is In about $17\%$ of all such random samples of $5$ patients, none of the patients would have missed an appointment. $P(X=0) \approx 0.1681$ is the long-run proportion of random samples of $5$ patients in which none of the patients missed an appointment.
The chance that any one of the patients in a sample missed an appointment is $17\%$ is incorrect: Confuses $P(X=0)$ with the probability for one individual item; the probability for one patient is given in the scenario.
In about $17\%$ of all such samples, all of the patients would have missed an appointment is incorrect: Reverses the event: $X=0$ means none are of the stated kind, not all.
Exactly $17\%$ of the patients in every sample of $5$ missed an appointment is incorrect: Reads a probability as a guaranteed percentage in every sample.
